concepts.title: Inflation
concepts.hook: Five ₹20 idlis fit a ₹100 note; after each idli becomes ₹25, only four fit. The note has not changed. What did?
concepts.rule: Inflation is the yearly rise in prices across a basket of everyday goods. When prices rise faster than your money, it buys less. India's central bank aims for about 4%.

claims.text: India uses a consumer price index to track change in a basket of retail prices.
A rise in broad prices cuts the buying power of cash if its amount stays fixed.
India's inflation rate compares the price of a basket in one month with the same month a year earlier, using prices collected from over 50,000 shops.
If income rises less than prices, real income falls; people on fixed incomes lose buying power.
India's inflation target is 4%, with a low limit of 2% and a top limit of 6%, set until March 2031.

items.stem: Your college fee rises 10% a year, while your family's income rises 5% a year. What happens over a few years?

options.text: The fee takes a bigger share of income.
options.feedback: The fee grows twice as fast as income, so each year it eats a larger part of it.

options.text: Nothing changes, since both keep rising.
options.feedback: Both rise, but at different speeds. The faster one, the fee, takes a growing share.

options.text: The fee gets easier to pay.
options.feedback: Income grows slower than the fee, so paying it gets harder each year, not easier.

items.stem: Riya can keep ₹20,000 at home or in a deposit paying 7% a year. Prices rise 5%. Which keeps its buying power?

options.feedback: It grows faster than prices, so after a year it buys a little more than today.
Cash at home stays at ₹20,000 while prices rise 5%, so it buys less each year.
Only the cash falls behind. A 7% deposit outpaces 5% price rises.

items.stem: A toy cost ₹385 last May and ₹410 this May. What is its inflation rate?

options.feedback: The rise is ₹25. Divide 25 by last May's ₹385 and multiply by 100 to get about 6.5%.
₹25 is the rise in rupees, not the percent. Divide it by ₹385 to get about 6.5%.
The decimal point slipped. 25 divided by 385 is about 0.065, which is 6.5%.

items.stem: How does India find out what prices are doing each month?

options.text: Survey staff note prices in 50,000+ shops.
options.feedback: Yes. Staff visit over 50,000 shops in 2,295 markets every month to record retail prices.

options.text: Shops send one price list a year.
options.feedback: Prices are recorded every month, not once a year, and survey staff collect them in person.

options.text: It guesses from a few big cities.
options.feedback: No guessing is involved. Prices come from over 50,000 shops across 2,295 markets.

items.stem: Why do people living on a fixed pension feel rising prices the most?

options.text: Their income stays put while prices climb.
options.feedback: A pension that never grows meets higher prices each year, so it buys less and less.
A fixed pension does not rise at all, so it falls behind when prices go up.
Their shopping may differ, but the main problem is income that stays fixed while prices rise.

items.stem: Pay counted in rupees is nominal pay. Pay counted by what it can buy is ___.

options.feedback: Pay measured by what it buys is called real pay. It shows how far the money really goes.
That is the nominal figure again, the rupee amount, not what the money can buy.
Last year's pay is still counted in rupees. Adjusting pay for prices gives real pay.

items.stem: A friend says any inflation at all means the economy is in trouble. What is wrong with that?

options.feedback: The RBI's target is 4% inflation, with a band of 2% to 6%, so mild inflation is planned.
The target is not zero. It is 4%, with a lower limit of 2%.
No target asks for fixed prices. India aims for steady rises of about 4% a year.

items.stem: Put these in order to work out an inflation rate.

options.text: Find this May's price and last May's price.
options.feedback: You need the same item's price in the same month, one year apart, before any sum.

options.text: Subtract to get the rise in rupees.
options.feedback: The gap between the two prices shows how many rupees more it costs now.

options.text: Divide the rise by last May's price, then multiply by 100.
options.feedback: Dividing by the older price turns the rupee rise into a percent, the inflation rate.

misconceptions.name: One price is the index
misconceptions.correction: One snack can rise while the broad basket moves in a different way.

misconceptions.name: Same cash, same goods
misconceptions.correction: When broad prices rise, the same cash can buy fewer goods.

misconceptions.name: Any raise makes you better off
misconceptions.correction: A raise smaller than the rise in prices still buys less than before.

misconceptions.name: The goal is zero inflation
misconceptions.correction: India's target is about 4%, inside a band of 2% to 6%.

steps.title: Inflation is prices rising across a basket

hook.stem: The news says retail inflation was 3% in May. What does that mean?

options.text: Everyday prices are about 3% above last May.
options.feedback: Right. It compares a big basket of everyday prices with the same month a year before.

options.text: Every single price rose by exactly 3%.
options.feedback: Some prices jump and some barely move. The 3% is the overall change across the basket.
The figure compares this May with last May, a full year apart, not with the month before.

steps.teach: Inflation is how much prices rose in a year. India checks a basket of everyday goods each month and compares it with the same month last year.

example.ask: Tap the comparison.
parts: Rice, milk and bus fares in the big list
cost 3% more than they did last May,
so the news reports 3% inflation.
example.spot: cost 3% more than they did last May,
example.feedback: Inflation compares the same basket with the same month a year earlier.

guided.stem: Onions double in price, but most other prices barely move. What happens to inflation?
guided.hint: Onions are one item in a very big basket.

options.feedback: Yes. One item doubling moves the whole basket only a little when the rest stays flat.
Onions are a small part of the basket, so the overall rise is far smaller than double.
A price went up and the others held still, so the basket costs a bit more, not less.

guided.stem: This June's inflation figure is out. Which prices does it compare?
guided.hint: Look for a gap of one full year.

options.feedback: Right. Matching the same month a year apart is how the rate is worked out.
A one-month gap is not used here. The rate compares the same month a year earlier.

options.text: This June against ten years ago.
options.feedback: Ten years is far too long a gap. The yearly rate compares with the same month last year.

steps.takeaway: Inflation is the yearly rise across a whole basket of prices.

steps.title: When prices outrun your money, it buys less

hook.stem: Your pocket money stays at ₹2,000 while prices rise 10%. What happens?

options.text: It buys about a tenth less.
options.feedback: Right. The note is the same, but each thing costs more, so the same money covers less.

options.text: It buys the same, since it is still ₹2,000.
options.feedback: The number on the money stays put, but prices moved up, so it now covers less shopping.
Higher prices work the other way. The same ₹2,000 now covers less, not more.

steps.teach: When prices rise, the same money buys less. If your income grows slower than prices, you can buy less than last year, even with a raise.

example.ask: Tap why she is behind.
parts: Kavya got a 5% raise this year,
but her rent and groceries cost 7% more,
so her pay now buys less than before.
example.spot: but her rent and groceries cost 7% more,
example.feedback: Her costs grew faster than her pay, so the raise did not keep up.

guided.stem: A ₹100 basket of shopping now costs ₹125. How much of it does ₹100 buy?
guided.hint: Work out 100 divided by 125.

options.feedback: Yes. 100 divided by 125 is 0.8, so the same cash covers 80% of the basket.
The basket now costs ₹125, more than you hold, so ₹100 cannot cover all of it.
That flips the sum. ₹125 is the new price, so ₹100 buys less than one basket.

guided.stem: Prices rise 5% this year. Whose pay keeps up?
guided.hint: Pay has to grow at least as fast as prices.

options.feedback: Right. His pay grew faster than prices, so it buys a little more than last year.
Her pay rose, but slower than prices, so it buys less than it did last year.
With no rise at all, his same pay meets higher prices and buys less.

steps.takeaway: If prices grow faster than your money, you fall behind.

steps.title: Idle cash shrinks, and the RBI aims for about 4%

hook.stem: What inflation rate do you think India's central bank aims for?

options.feedback: Right. The RBI's target is 4%, with a band from 2% to 6% around it.
The target is not zero. India aims for about 4%, inside a band of 2% to 6%.
That would be far above the band. The upper limit is 6%, and the target is 4%.

steps.teach: Money that earns nothing loses buying power each year. India's central bank aims to keep inflation near 4%, inside a band of 2% to 6%.

example.ask: Tap what happens to the cash.
parts: Dadaji keeps ₹50,000 under his mattress for years,
and each year it buys a little less,
because prices keep rising around it.
example.spot: and each year it buys a little less,
example.feedback: The cash never changes, but rising prices make it worth a little less each year.

guided.stem: ₹10,000 sits in a cupboard for a year while prices rise 5%. What does it buy next year?
guided.hint: The cash stays still while prices move up.

options.feedback: Yes. 10,000 divided by 1.05 is about 9,520, so it buys a bit less than now.
Prices rose 5% while the cash stayed the same, so it buys less than it does today.
Cash in a cupboard earns nothing. Rising prices make it buy less, not more.

guided.stem: Inflation comes in at 7% this year. Where is that against the RBI's band?
guided.hint: The band runs from 2% to 6%.

options.feedback: Right. 7% is higher than the 6% upper limit of the band.
The target is 4%. At 7%, inflation is above even the 6% upper limit.
The lower limit is 2%. A rate of 7% is well above the whole band.

steps.takeaway: Idle cash shrinks; India aims for about 4% inflation.

concepts.title: Compounding
concepts.hook: ₹1 lakh growing at a made-up 7% for 30 years becomes about ₹7.6 lakh. The last ten years add more than the first twenty.
concepts.rule: Compounding means a gain can earn a later gain when it stays in the pot. A SIP adds money at set times, but that does not promise a set return.

claims.text: Compound growth includes growth on past gains as well as the starting amount.
A SIP is a way to add money at set times; market returns are not fixed.
Saved at 5% a year, 365 grows to about 466 after five years and about 1,578 after thirty years.
The sooner saving starts, the more time compound interest has to build it up.

items.stem: ₹2,000 earns compound interest at 10% a year, with nothing taken out. About what is it worth after two years?

options.feedback: Year one adds ₹200 to make ₹2,200. Year two adds 10% of ₹2,200, which is ₹220.
That adds ₹200 twice. In year two the 10% works on ₹2,200, so it adds ₹220.
That is the value after one year. A second year of 10% takes it to about ₹2,420.

items.stem: Tanvi says ₹1,000 at 10% a year for three years adds exactly ₹300 if gains stay in. What is she missing?

options.text: Each year, 10% works on a bigger sum.
options.feedback: Kept gains grow the base, so the years add ₹100, ₹110 and ₹121. That is ₹331, not ₹300.

options.text: The 10% counts only in the first year.
options.feedback: The rate applies every year. Each year it works on the sum plus the gains kept in.

options.text: Interest is paid only at the very end.
options.feedback: Here gains are added each year and stay in, so later years earn on them too.

items.stem: Put one year of compound growth in order.

options.text: Work out the interest on the balance.
options.feedback: The gain for the year comes from the rate times the money now in the pot.

options.text: Add that interest to the balance.
options.feedback: Leaving the gain in makes the pot bigger than it was at the start.

options.text: Use the new balance for next year's interest.
options.feedback: Next year the rate works on the bigger pot, so the gain grows too.

items.stem: Riya puts ₹10,000 away at age 15. Dev puts the same away at 20. Same rate, no withdrawals. Who has more at 30?

options.text: Riya, with five more years of growth.
options.feedback: Her money grows for fifteen years and his for ten, so hers has longer to build on gains.

options.text: Dev, since his money is newer.
options.feedback: Newer money has had less time to grow. At the same rate, more years give more.

options.text: Both have the same, since the sum matches.
options.feedback: The sums match, but Riya's grows for five extra years, and those gains earn gains too.

items.stem: At the same steady rate, why do the last ten years of saving add more than the first ten?

options.text: Later gains work on a bigger pot.
options.feedback: By then the pot holds years of kept gains, so the same rate adds more rupees.

options.text: Rates rise as savers get older.
options.feedback: The rate here stays the same. The pot is bigger, so each year adds more.

options.text: Banks pay a bonus to long savers.
options.feedback: No bonus is needed. Growth on a bigger, older pot is what makes later years add more.

items.stem: Which ends with more at 8% a year: ₹10,000 left for 20 years, or ₹20,000 left for 10 years?

options.feedback: It grows to about ₹46,600. The ₹20,000 grows to about ₹43,200, as it has half the time.
Starting bigger helps, but ten extra years of growth on growth help more here.

options.text: Both end the same, since 10,000 × 20 equals 20,000 × 10.
options.feedback: Growth is not sum times years. Extra years multiply, so the longer one ends higher.

items.stem: Putting a set sum into a fund at set times, like ₹500 each month, is called a ___.

options.feedback: A systematic investment plan, or SIP, is a way to invest a set sum at set times.
A lump sum goes in all at once. Here money goes in bit by bit each month.
A fixed deposit locks one sum at a bank rate. Monthly sums into a fund make a SIP.

items.stem: Kiran pays ₹500 into her SIP every month. Then the market falls this year. What happens to her fund's value?

options.text: It can fall, even with every payment made.
options.feedback: Her payments are regular, but the fund's value still moves with the market.

options.text: It must rise, because she paid on time.
options.feedback: Paying on time sets her habit. It does not set what the market does.

options.text: It stays flat until prices recover.
options.feedback: A fund's value moves with what it holds. When prices fall, its value can fall too.

misconceptions.name: Gain only on start
misconceptions.correction: When gains stay in the pot, later gains can build on them too.

misconceptions.name: SIP means sure gain
misconceptions.correction: A SIP sets a payment pattern; it does not set market returns.

misconceptions.name: A late start costs nothing
misconceptions.correction: Starting later gives money fewer years to grow, so it ends smaller.

steps.title: Gains start earning gains

hook.stem: Sana and Om each save ₹1,000 at 10%. Sana leaves her interest in; Om spends his. Who has more after two years?

options.feedback: Right. Her ₹100 gain stayed in and earned ₹10 more in year two.
Om has ₹1,000 plus ₹200 spent. Sana's kept gain earned extra, so she has ₹1,210.
Spending the interest means it cannot earn more. Sana ends with ₹1,210 saved.

steps.teach: With compound interest, you earn on your savings and on the interest they already made. So each year's gain is a bit bigger.

example.ask: Tap the interest on interest.
parts: Meera's ₹1,000 earned ₹100 in year one.
In year two, that ₹100 earned ₹10 of its own,
so her gain grew from ₹100 to ₹110.
example.spot: In year two, that ₹100 earned ₹10 of its own,
example.feedback: The ₹10 came from last year's gain, not from her first ₹1,000.

guided.stem: ₹500 earns 10% a year and the gain stays in. What is it worth after one year?
guided.hint: Find 10% of ₹500 and add it.

options.feedback: Yes. 10% of ₹500 is ₹50, so the pot is now ₹550.
That adds only ₹10. 10% of ₹500 is ₹50, which makes ₹550.
That adds ₹100, which is 20%. At 10% the gain is ₹50.

guided.stem: In year two, the ₹550 earns 10% again. How big is the new gain?
guided.hint: Work out 10% of the new total, not of the first ₹500.

options.feedback: Right. The rate now works on ₹550, so the gain grows to ₹55.
That is 10% of the old ₹500. The pot is now ₹550, so the gain is ₹55.
That is only the gain on last year's gain. The full gain is 10% of ₹550, or ₹55.

steps.takeaway: Gains you leave in start to earn gains too.

steps.title: Time does most of the work

hook.stem: You save ₹365 once at 5% a year and leave it. About how much is it after 30 years?

options.feedback: Right. Growth on growth for 30 years takes ₹365 to about ₹1,578.
That counts 5% of ₹365 each year, as if gains never earned. Compounding gives about ₹1,578.
That is the value after five years. Twenty-five more years take it near ₹1,578.

steps.teach: Growth on growth is slow at first and fast later. Saved at 5%, ₹365 is about ₹466 after five years, but about ₹1,578 after thirty.

example.ask: Tap why Asha ends with more.
parts: Asha and Rohan both save at the same rate,
but Asha starts ten years sooner,
so her money has longer to grow.
example.spot: but Asha starts ten years sooner,
example.feedback: The same rate gives more when it has more years to work on past gains.

guided.stem: Asha leaves ₹1,000 at 8% for 10 years. Ben leaves ₹1,000 at 8% for 20 years. How do they compare?
guided.hint: Ten more years of growth work on a bigger pot.

options.text: Ben has about twice as much.
options.feedback: Yes. Asha reaches about ₹2,160; Ben reaches about ₹4,660.
That counts ₹80 a year with no growth on growth. Ben ends with about twice as much.
Ben's money grows for ten more years, so he ends with far more.

guided.stem: Over 30 years at 5%, which five years add the most rupees?
guided.hint: The pot is biggest near the end.

options.feedback: Right. By then the pot is largest, so the same 5% adds the most rupees.
The pot is smallest then, so 5% adds the fewest rupees.

options.text: All five-year spans add the same.
options.feedback: Each span starts from a bigger pot, so later spans add more.

steps.takeaway: The longer money grows, the faster it grows.

steps.title: A SIP is a habit, not a promise

hook.stem: A SIP takes ₹500 from your account every month. What does it fix?

options.text: How much goes in, and when.
options.feedback: Right. A SIP sets the sum and the dates. The market sets the return.
A SIP does not fix the return. The fund's value moves with the market.

options.text: That the fund only goes up.
options.feedback: Funds can fall as well as rise. A SIP just keeps adding money on set dates.

steps.teach: A SIP puts in the same sum at set times, like ₹500 each month. It sets your habit. It does not set what the market pays back.

example.ask: Tap the part a SIP cannot promise.
parts: Ravi sets up a ₹1,000 SIP each month,
the money goes in on the 5th,
and the fund's value moves with the market.
example.spot: and the fund's value moves with the market.
example.feedback: Ravi controls the sum and the date. The market decides how the fund's value moves.

guided.stem: A friend says a SIP fund is safe because money goes in every month. What is mixed up?
guided.hint: Ask what the regular part controls.

options.text: Paying often does not fix returns.
options.feedback: Yes. Regular payments set a habit. The fund can still fall.
A SIP takes money again and again. The mix-up is about returns.

options.text: Nothing; monthly payments make it safe.
options.feedback: Monthly payments do not stop a fund from falling in a bad year.

guided.stem: Which of these does a ₹500 SIP set for you?
guided.hint: Think of what you choose when you sign up.

options.feedback: Right. You pick the sum and the dates when you start.
No one can set that. The market decides the return.
A SIP has no say over how high or low the fund goes.

steps.takeaway: A SIP fixes what you put in, not what you get back.

concepts.title: The rule of 72
concepts.hook: At a made-up 9% rate, 72 ÷ 9 says eight years to double. Working it out exactly gives close to eight, but not exactly eight.
concepts.rule: For a steady percent rate, divide 72 by the rate to guess the years to double. It works for unpaid debt too. It is a rough shortcut, not a promise of market growth.

claims.text: The rule of 72 is a rough way to guess when a sum may double. Divide 72 by a set rate.
Market returns do not have a fixed rate, so the shortcut is only a what-if tool there.
At 4% a year, savings double in about 18 years, since 72 divided by 4 is 18.
The rule works for debt too: an unpaid card balance at 18% interest doubles in about four years.

items.stem: A savings account pays a steady 2% a year. By the rule of 72, about how many years until the money doubles?

options.feedback: Divide 72 by 2 to get 36. At a slow rate, doubling takes a long time.
The rate is not the time. Dividing 72 by 2 gives about 36 years.
That multiplies 72 by 2. The rule divides 72 by the rate, giving 36.

items.stem: To double money in 6 years, the rule needs a steady rate of 72 ÷ 6 = ___.

options.feedback: Working backwards, 72 divided by 6 years gives a 12% yearly rate.
At 6% the rule gives 12 years. To halve that time, the rate must be 12%.
That multiplies 72 by 6. Dividing gives the rate: 12% a year.

items.stem: On a train, Arjun's uncle says his deposit rate is going up from 6% to 8%. What happens to its doubling time?

options.feedback: A higher rate means fewer years. 72 ÷ 8 is 9, down from 72 ÷ 6, which is 12.
More growth each year gets money to double sooner, not later.
The doubling time depends on the rate. At 8% it drops to about 9 years.

items.stem: A college student owes ₹8,000 at 12% a year and pays nothing back. About when will she owe ₹16,000?

options.feedback: Unpaid debt grows like savings do. 72 ÷ 12 is 6, so it doubles in about six years.
The rate is not the time. 72 divided by 12 gives about six years.

options.text: Never, if she borrows no more.
options.feedback: Interest keeps adding to an unpaid sum, so it grows even with no new borrowing.

items.stem: Ishan has ₹10,000 saved at 6% and owes ₹10,000 at 18%. After about 12 years, how do the two compare?

options.text: The debt ends up several times bigger.
options.feedback: Savings double once in 12 years. The debt doubles about three times, so it ends far bigger.

options.text: Both end up the same size.
options.feedback: They start the same, but 18% doubles every four years while 6% takes twelve.
The savings grow more slowly. 18% makes the debt grow about three times as fast.

items.stem: Why does paying only a small part of a card bill each month let the debt keep growing?

options.text: The unpaid part keeps earning interest.
options.feedback: The part you leave unpaid is charged interest too, so the bill can keep growing.

options.text: Cards stop charging once you pay something.
options.feedback: Any amount left unpaid is still charged interest, month after month.

options.text: Interest is charged only on new buys.
options.feedback: The old unpaid balance is charged too, which is why it can keep growing.

items.stem: How would you sum up when the rule of 72 works well?

options.text: When the rate stays the same each year.
options.feedback: The rule turns one steady rate into a rough doubling time.
It works best for steady rates, like a fixed deposit, not for jumpy share prices.

options.text: For any return, even a jumpy one.
options.feedback: A return that jumps around has no single rate to divide by.

items.stem: Kabir says a fund that averaged 9% over ten years doubled in exactly eight. What is the mistake?

options.text: An average hides ups and downs.
options.feedback: Real returns changed each year, so the time to double can differ from 72 ÷ 9.
The sum is right: 72 ÷ 9 is 8. The flaw is using it on returns that were not steady.

options.text: Funds always double sooner than the rule.
options.feedback: No such rule exists. Uneven returns can make doubling take longer or shorter.

misconceptions.name: Exact clock
misconceptions.correction: The rule gives a rough guess, not an exact date.

misconceptions.name: Any market rate is fixed
misconceptions.correction: Market gains can vary; the shortcut needs a steady assumed rate.

misconceptions.name: Debt stays the same size
misconceptions.correction: Unpaid debt gathers interest too, and a high rate doubles it fast.

steps.title: Divide 72 by the rate

hook.stem: Money grows at a steady 6% a year. About how long until it doubles?

options.feedback: Right. 72 divided by 6 is 12, so about 12 years at a steady 6%.
That uses the rate as the years. Divide 72 by 6 to get about 12.
72 is the number you divide, not the answer. 72 ÷ 6 gives about 12 years.

steps.teach: To guess how long money takes to double, divide 72 by the yearly rate. At 8%, 72 ÷ 8 is 9, so about nine years.

example.ask: Tap the shortcut sum.
parts: Nisha's savings grow at a steady 4% a year.
She works out 72 ÷ 4 = 18,
so they double in about 18 years.
example.spot: She works out 72 ÷ 4 = 18,
example.feedback: Dividing 72 by the rate gives the rough number of years to double.

guided.stem: A deposit pays a steady 9%. Roughly how many years to double?
guided.hint: Work out 72 divided by 9.

options.feedback: Yes. 72 ÷ 9 is 8, so about eight years.
Nine is the rate. Dividing 72 by 9 gives about 8 years.
That multiplies 9 by 9. The rule divides 72 by 9.

guided.stem: Which rate doubles money in about 6 years?
guided.hint: Try 72 divided by each rate.

options.feedback: Right. 72 ÷ 12 is 6.
At 6%, 72 ÷ 6 gives 12 years, not 6.
At 72%, money would double in about one year by the rule.

steps.takeaway: Years to double is about 72 divided by the rate.

steps.title: Debt doubles the same way

hook.stem: A card balance of ₹10,000 is left unpaid at 18% a year. About when does it reach ₹20,000?

options.feedback: Right. 72 ÷ 18 is 4, so unpaid card debt doubles in about four years.
The rate is not the years. 72 divided by 18 gives about four.
Interest keeps adding to the unpaid balance, so it grows on its own.

steps.teach: The rule works on debt too. An unpaid card balance at 18% doubles in about four years, since 72 ÷ 18 is 4.

parts: Mahi's fund follows a big index,
so it holds the firms on that list in the same mix,
and no one picks favourites.
example.spot: so it holds the firms on that list in the same mix,
example.feedback: The index list sets what the fund holds and how much of each.

guided.stem: A company joins the index. What does the index fund do?
guided.hint: The fund follows the list.

options.feedback: Yes. The fund copies the index, so a new member joins the fund.
Ignoring changes would stop the fund matching the index.
One new member does not change the rest. The fund just adds it.

guided.stem: An index gives Firm A twice the weight of Firm B. In the fund, how does A compare with B?
guided.hint: Same proportions as the index.

options.text: Twice as much A as B.
options.feedback: Right. The fund holds each firm in the same proportion as the index.
The fund copies the index's weights, so A gets twice as much.
That flips the index's mix. The fund keeps A at twice B.

steps.takeaway: An index fund holds the index's firms in the index's mix.

steps.title: No picking means lower costs

hook.stem: Why are index funds usually cheaper to run than active funds?

options.text: No one is paid to pick shares.
options.feedback: Right. Following a list takes little research or trading, so the fee is lower.
Index funds do charge a fee. It is just lower, since there is little to manage.
Many hold more firms than active funds. The saving comes from not picking.

steps.teach: Active funds pay managers to pick shares. Index funds just follow a list, with little trading. So their yearly fee, the expense ratio, is usually lower.

example.ask: Tap why the fee is lower.
parts: Kunal's index fund rarely trades,
because it only follows its list,
so it charges a lower fee.
example.spot: because it only follows its list,
example.feedback: With no stock picking and little trading, the fund costs less to run.

guided.stem: Fund X charges 1% a year and Fund Y charges 0.2%. Both follow the same index. Which keeps more of the index's return?
guided.hint: The fee comes out of the return.

options.feedback: Yes. Its lower fee takes less out, so more of the index's return stays with you.
Fund X takes 1% a year, five times more than Y, so it keeps less.
They follow the same index, but X's bigger fee leaves less behind.

guided.stem: What is an expense ratio?
guided.hint: It is counted each year.

options.text: The share of a fund's money taken each year for costs.
options.feedback: Right. It is a yearly percent of the fund used to pay its running costs.
No fund promises a return. The expense ratio is a cost, not a gain.
It is not paid once. It is taken every year from the fund's money.

steps.takeaway: No stock picking keeps index fund fees low.

steps.title: It follows the index, ups and downs, a little behind

hook.stem: The index rises 10% in a year. About what does an index fund on it return?

options.feedback: Right. It follows the index, but its fees keep it slightly behind.
Fees and running costs leave a small gap, so it lands a little under.
An index fund aims to match its index, not beat it.

steps.teach: An index fund rises and falls with its index. Fees and running costs keep it a little behind. That small gap is called tracking error.

visual.label: Example: index up 10% in a year

example.ask: Tap what shows it falls with the index.
parts: The index fell 8% this year,
and Lata's index fund fell about 8.2%,
a small gap left by its fees.
example.spot: and Lata's index fund fell about 8.2%,
example.feedback: An index fund copies its index both ways, so a falling index pulls it down too, plus fees.

guided.stem: The market index falls 15%. What happens to an index fund that follows it?
guided.hint: The fund copies the index both ways.

options.feedback: Yes. It holds the same shares, so it falls with the index.

options.text: It stays safe, since funds are spread.
options.feedback: A spread across the index still falls when the whole index falls.

options.text: It rises, since managers step in.
options.feedback: No manager steps in. The fund simply follows the index down.

guided.stem: An index rose 12% and its fund rose 11.7%. What is the 0.3% gap called?
guided.hint: It is the gap between fund and index.

options.feedback: Right. Tracking error is the slight gap left by expenses and running costs.
A dividend is a payout from profit. The gap has its own name.
Inflation is prices rising. The gap between fund and index is tracking error.

steps.takeaway: An index fund matches its index, up and down, minus a small gap.

concepts.title: UPI scams and social engineering
concepts.hook: A fake prize message may ask for a UPI PIN to make a payment look like a receipt.
concepts.rule: A scam story can steer a person to approve a payment. A UPI PIN approves payments; receiving never needs it. No one else needs your PIN or OTP.

claims.text: NPCI warns that a QR scan and UPI PIN can be used to make a payment, not collect a prize.
A collect request asks the payer to approve money leaving an account.
RBI says getting money never needs a QR scan or a PIN, so take care if asked for either.
RBI says never share your UPI PIN or OTP with anyone, not even bank staff.
RBI says to tell your bank at once about a debit you did not make, and block debits, including UPI.

items.stem: Why is a request to scan a QR code to receive money a warning sign?

options.text: Receiving money needs no scan at all.
options.feedback: RBI says getting money never needs a QR scan or a PIN, so this is a trick.

options.text: QR codes only work in shops.
options.feedback: QR codes work anywhere. The point is that receiving money never needs one.
Speed is not the issue. A scan starts a payment out of your account.

items.stem: Match each UPI action to which way the money moves.

options.feedback: In a payment, your PIN is your approval, so money leaves your account.
Money only leaves when you approve with your PIN.
When a friend sends you money, you do nothing but receive it.
Getting money needs no PIN and no scan from you.

items.stem: A caller from a 'college fest' says to scan a QR code for your ₹500 prize. What do the scan and PIN really do?

options.feedback: Scanning and entering a PIN approve a payment. A real prize would need neither.
Money coming in needs no scan or PIN. This sets up a payment out.
Here the PIN approves a payment out. A prize check would never need it.

items.stem: A scammer sends three UPI collect requests of ₹1,500 each, all marked 'cashback'. If you approve all three with your PIN, about how much leaves?

options.feedback: Each approval pays ₹1,500. Three times ₹1,500 is ₹4,500 out of your account.
Collect requests take money. Each approval sends ₹1,500 out, not in.
The cashback label is the bait. Each approval is a real payment of ₹1,500.

items.stem: A UPI request in which someone asks you to send them money is called a ___ request.

options.feedback: A collect request asks you to pay, and your PIN approves that payment.
Scammers may label it a refund, but the request type is collect.
Nothing is received. The request asks you to pay, so it is a collect request.

items.stem: Sam says he can approve a collect request just to see what it is, then cancel it later. What is wrong?

options.text: Approving with his PIN is the payment itself.
options.feedback: Once he enters his PIN, the money is sent. Declining is the only way to stop it.

options.text: Collect requests can always be undone.
options.feedback: There is no undo button once the PIN approves it. The money has gone.
The amount shows before approval. Entering the PIN pays it.

items.stem: In the hostel, a caller claiming to be from your bank says your account will be blocked unless you share the OTP just sent. What is this?

options.text: A common fraud trick, so share nothing.
options.feedback: RBI says threats about blocking your account are a common trick, and an OTP is never shared.
Banks do not ask for your OTP. RBI warns never to share it, even with bank staff.

options.text: Safe, since the OTP came from the bank.
options.feedback: The OTP is real, which is why the scammer wants it. Sharing it lets him in.

items.stem: Which line best sums up how to stay safe from UPI tricks?

options.text: Keep your PIN and OTP secret; receiving needs neither.
options.feedback: These two RBI rules guard against the tricks in this lesson, where people pay by mistake.

options.text: Share your PIN only with bank staff.
options.feedback: RBI says never share it, not even with bank officials.

options.text: Approve requests first, then check them.
options.feedback: Approving is paying. Check first, and decline anything you did not expect.

misconceptions.name: PIN to receive
misconceptions.correction: To get money, a person need not key in a UPI PIN.

misconceptions.name: Official tone proves safety
misconceptions.correction: A neat bank-like note can still tell a false story.

misconceptions.name: Bank staff may know your PIN
misconceptions.correction: No one, not even bank staff, needs your PIN or OTP.

misconceptions.name: Approve now, cancel later
misconceptions.correction: Entering your PIN on a collect request is the payment itself.

steps.title: Your PIN sends money; it never receives it

hook.stem: A buyer on a resale site says, 'Scan my QR code and enter your PIN to get paid.' What will happen?

options.feedback: Right. Getting money never needs a scan or a PIN, so this sends money out.
Receiving needs no PIN at all. Entering it approves a payment from you.

options.text: Nothing, it only checks your account.
options.feedback: Entering your PIN on this request approves a payment, not a simple check.

steps.teach: Getting money on UPI needs no PIN and no QR scan. Your PIN approves money going out. So a request to enter it to get paid is a trick.

example.ask: Tap the red flag.
parts: Ankit sells his old cycle online,
and the buyer asks him to enter his UPI PIN
to receive the ₹3,000.
example.spot: and the buyer asks him to enter his UPI PIN
example.feedback: Receiving money never needs a PIN, so this request is a trick to make him pay.

guided.stem: You are getting a ₹500 refund. What do you need to type in?
guided.hint: Think about which way the money moves.

options.text: Nothing, since money coming in needs no PIN.
options.feedback: Yes. Money coming to you needs no PIN and no scan.
A PIN approves money going out. A refund coming in needs none.
No OTP is needed to receive money. Never share one with anyone.

guided.stem: A message says 'Scan to claim your ₹1,000 prize.' What does the scan really start?
guided.hint: Receiving never needs a scan.

options.feedback: Right. Scanning a QR code starts a payment, so the prize story is a trick.
Money coming in needs no scan. The scan sets up a payment out.
A QR scan does not check balances. It starts a payment.

steps.takeaway: Your PIN approves payments. Receiving money never needs it.

steps.title: A collect request asks you to pay

hook.stem: A collect request pops up in your UPI app with a 'cashback' note. If you enter your PIN, what happens?

options.text: You pay the person who sent it.
options.feedback: Right. A collect request asks for your money, and the PIN approves it.
A collect request takes money from you. The cashback note is the bait.
Entering the PIN approves it. Declining is how you cancel.

steps.teach: A collect request is someone asking you for money. Entering your PIN approves the payment. Scammers dress it up as a prize, refund or cashback.

example.ask: Tap the trick.
parts: Divya gets a request marked 'Prize ₹2,000',
with a note saying 'Enter PIN to receive',
but it is really asking her to pay ₹2,000.
example.spot: with a note saying 'Enter PIN to receive',
example.feedback: RBI warns that scammers write 'enter PIN to receive' on a collect request, which takes money out.

guided.stem: Who pays when you approve a collect request with your PIN?
guided.hint: Collect means someone is collecting from you.

options.feedback: Yes. Approving a collect request sends your money to the one who asked.
The sender is asking for money, not giving it.
The bank moves your own money. You are the one who pays.

guided.stem: A collect request says 'Refund ₹750', but you were not expecting any refund. What is the safe move?
guided.hint: Approving means paying.

options.feedback: Right. Declining stops the payment, and a real refund never needs your PIN.

options.text: Approve it to see what happens.
options.feedback: Approving with your PIN is the payment itself, so ₹750 would leave you.
By then the money has gone. Decline first instead.

steps.takeaway: Approving a collect request with your PIN always means you pay.

steps.title: Keep your PIN secret, and act fast if tricked

hook.stem: A caller says he is from your bank and needs your UPI PIN to update your KYC. What is the right reply?

options.text: Refuse, since no one needs your PIN.
options.feedback: Right. RBI says never share your PIN, not even with bank staff.

options.text: Share it, since he knows your name.
options.feedback: Scammers often know names. Knowing yours does not make him safe.
Any part of your PIN helps a scammer. Keep all of it to yourself.

steps.teach: Never share your UPI PIN or OTP with anyone. That includes callers who say they are bank staff, however real they sound.

right.title: Unsafe
lines: Read out a PIN or OTP

example.ask: Tap the mistake.
parts: Manav finds a 'bank helpline' through a web search,
the man who answers asks for his OTP,
and Manav reads it out to him.
example.spot: and Manav reads it out to him.
example.feedback: Sharing an OTP hands over control. RBI warns never to share it, even with bank staff.

guided.stem: Who is allowed to know your UPI PIN?
guided.hint: It is yours alone.

options.feedback: Yes. No bank worker or helpline ever needs your PIN.
RBI says not even bank officials should get your PIN.
Real or fake, customer care has no need for your PIN.

guided.stem: You get a debit SMS for a payment you never made. What does RBI say to do?
guided.hint: Speed matters.

options.text: Tell your bank at once and block UPI debits.
options.feedback: Right. Quick action can stop more money leaving your account.

options.text: Wait a week to see if it returns.
options.feedback: Waiting gives a scammer time. RBI says tell your bank at once.

options.text: Reply to the SMS with your PIN.
options.feedback: Never send your PIN anywhere. Contact your bank directly.

steps.takeaway: Your PIN and OTP are for you alone, never for callers.
